name: Masala Hash Browns
description: Crispy, golden potato hash browns given an Indian twist with warming spices, green chilli, and coriander — a fun fusion breakfast side.

items.name: Potato
items.preparation: medium, starchy like Maris Piper, peeled and coarsely grated

items.name: Carom seeds (ajwain)
items.preparation: ( optional — helps digestion and adds flavour)

steps: Grate and drain: Coarsely grate the potatoes into a large bowl of cold water (this prevents browning and rinses off excess surface starch). Swish briefly, then drain thoroughly.

Remove moisture: Transfer the grated potato to a clean kitchen towel or muslin cloth and squeeze out as much water as possible — this step is essential for crispy hash browns rather than soggy ones. Let it sit for 10 minutes, then squeeze again.

Season the mixture: In a large bowl, combine the drained potato with the onion, green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds, turmeric, red chilli powder, garam masala, ajwain (if using), and coriander leaves. Mix well.

Bind: Sprinkle over the gram flour or cornflour and salt, then mix thoroughly until the mixture holds together when pressed — it shouldn't be wet or loose. If it still feels too wet, add another ½ tbsp of gram flour.

Shape: Divide the mixture into 8 portions. Take each portion in your palms and press firmly into a flat, compact patty about the size of your palm — the tighter you pack it, the better it holds together while frying.
Heat the oil: Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a wide, flat pan or griddle on medium heat.

Fry the hash browns: Place 3–4 patties in the pan at a time, without overcrowding. Cook for 4–5 minutes per side, pressing down gently once with a spatula, until deep golden brown and crisp on both sides. Add the remaining oil as needed for the second batch.
Drain and serve: Transfer to a plate lined with kitchen paper to remove excess oil. Serve hot, as is or with ketchup, mint chutney, or a dollop of yoghurt.

egg_check_notes: This recipe is naturally egg-free — gram flour (besan) or cornflour is used as the binder instead of egg, which is what many Western hash brown or patty recipes rely on. No hidden-egg risk here as long as you stick to gram flour/cornflour rather than a shop-bought binder mix (some ready-made "hash brown mixes" or coatings can contain egg powder, so always check if using a packet product).
nutrition_basis: Estimate only — not lab-tested. Based on 2 hash browns per serving.
common_mistakes: Skipping the water-squeezing step is the most common cause of hash browns falling apart or turning soggy and oily rather than crisp — don't rush this part. Also avoid flipping too early; let a proper golden crust form first so the patty holds its shape.
uk_sourcing_notes: Maris Piper or King Edward potatoes (widely available at any UK supermarket) work best due to their higher starch content, which helps crispiness. Ajwain is available at Indian grocers; if you don't have it, it can simply be left out without much impact on the dish.
storage_notes: The shaped (uncooked) patties can be covered and refrigerated for a few hours before frying. Cooked hash browns are best eaten fresh and crisp, but leftovers can be reheated in a dry pan or air fryer to re-crisp — avoid the microwave, which makes them soggy.
kid_friendly_notes: Omit the green chilli and reduce the red chilli powder for a milder, kid-friendly version — the cumin and garam masala still give plenty of flavour without heat.
